title: What license, certificate and periodic checks does an EU train driver need?
seoTitle: EU train driver license and certificate
description: Directive 2007/59/EC explained: the 10 year train driver license, the employer certificate, three yearly route and rolling stock checks and B1 language rules.
shortAnswer: Under Directive 2007/59/EC, every train driver on the EU railway system needs two documents: a license issued by the national safety authority, valid for 10 years, covering medical fitness, basic education and general professional knowledge; and a certificate issued by the employing railway undertaking or infrastructure manager for specific routes and rolling stock. Certificate holders must be rechecked at least every three years on rolling stock, infrastructure and, for non-native speakers, language.
keyTakeaways: Article 4 of Directive 2007/59/EC requires two documents: a license valid throughout the EU and one or more certificates valid only for the infrastructure and rolling stock named on them.
The minimum license age is 20, or 18 for a license limited to the issuing Member State; applicants need nine years of education and basic training equivalent to level 3 (Articles 10 and 11).
A license is valid for 10 years, and medical examinations are due at least every three years up to age 55 and every year after that (Article 14(5) and Annex II).

Annex VII sets minimum periodic checks of every three years for rolling stock knowledge, infrastructure knowledge and, for non-native speakers, language, with route and language checks also due after an absence of more than one year.

Drivers who must communicate with the infrastructure manager in its language need level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, subject to time-limited pilot project derogations.
regulator: European Parliament and Council of the European Union through Directive 2007/59/EC, applied by each Member State's national safety authority (the competent authority) with the European Union Agency for Railways
appliesTo: Train drivers operating locomotives and trains for railway undertakings that need a safety certificate
Train drivers working for infrastructure managers that need a safety authorization
Railway undertakings and infrastructure managers that issue certificates and run driver monitoring
Accredited or recognized training centers, examiners, doctors and psychologists

sections.heading: Why does an EU train driver need both a license and a certificate?

blocks.text: The license proves general fitness and competence that travels with the driver anywhere in the EU, while the certificate proves competence on a particular railway's routes and trains. Article 4 of [Directive 2007/59/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02007L0059-20190708) splits the two deliberately.

blocks.text: When a driver leaves, Article 17 makes the certificate invalid, but the driver receives a certified copy of it and of all documents evidencing their training, qualifications, experience and professional competences. The new employer must take those documents into account when issuing its own certificate, which is a direct argument for keeping driver training records in a portable, well structured form.

sections.heading: What are the minimum requirements for a train driver license?

blocks.text: Applicants must meet age, education, medical, psychological and general knowledge requirements before the competent authority issues a license, which it must do within one month of receiving all documents.

items: **Age:** at least 20 years, or 18 years with validity limited to the issuing Member State (Article 10).
**Education:** at least nine years of primary and secondary education and basic training equivalent to level 3 under Council Decision 85/368/EEC (Article 11(1)).
**Medical fitness:** an examination by an accredited or recognized doctor covering the criteria in Annex II (Article 11(2)).
**Occupational psychological fitness:** an examination by an accredited or recognized psychologist or doctor (Article 11(3)).
**General professional competence:** an examination covering at least the general subjects in Annex IV (Article 11(4)).

blocks.text: Annex IV lists seven general subjects. The first, on the driver's work and responsibilities, expects drivers to understand behaviors compatible with safety critical work, explicitly naming medication, alcohol, drugs and other psychoactive substances, illness, stress and fatigue. Member States may set stricter license requirements on their own territory but must still recognize licenses issued elsewhere (Article 9(2)).

sections.heading: What must a driver show to obtain and keep a certificate?

blocks.text: A certificate requires a valid license plus passed examinations on the specific rolling stock and infrastructure, language competence where needed, and training in the employer's safety management system. These requirements sit in Articles 12 and 13.

items: Rolling stock knowledge covering at least the subjects in Annex V (Article 13(1)).
Infrastructure knowledge, including route knowledge and operating rules, covering at least Annex VI (Article 13(2)).

Language: drivers who must communicate with the infrastructure manager on critical safety issues need level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages in that language (Annex VI, point 8).
Training by the railway undertaking or infrastructure manager in its safety management system (Article 13(3)).

blocks.text: Under Article 23, general, language and rolling stock training must be delivered by persons or bodies accredited or recognized under Article 20, and infrastructure training must be delivered by persons or bodies accredited or recognized by the Member State where the infrastructure is located. Annex III requires a good balance of theory and practice, accepts computer aided training for operational rules and signaling, and favors accompanied journeys by day and night for route knowledge.

sections.heading: How often must train drivers be rechecked?

blocks.text: License holders face recurring medical checks, and certificate holders face recurring knowledge checks at frequencies set by their employer's safety management system that must meet the Annex VII minimums. Article 16 links both to continued validity.

blocks.text: For each check, the issuing body must confirm by a statement on the certificate and in its register that the driver met the requirements. If a check is missed or failed, the monitoring procedure in Article 18 applies, which can lead to suspension. Article 23(8) also requires a process of continuous training so that staff competences are maintained between formal checks, which is where an employer's own [refresh cycle](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles) design matters.

sections.heading: What must railway undertakings and infrastructure managers do?

blocks.text: Employers must verify that every driver's license and certificate is valid, run a monitoring system, keep a certificate register and act immediately when monitoring calls competence into question. These duties are set out in Articles 15, 18 and 22.

items: Set up procedures for issuing and updating certificates within the safety management system, with an appeals procedure for drivers (Article 15).
Update a certificate without delay when the driver gains additional rolling stock or infrastructure authorizations (Article 15).
Keep a register of all certificates issued, renewed, suspended or withdrawn, including the data on periodic checks (Article 22(2)).

Ensure drivers are never under the influence of any substance likely to affect concentration, attention or behavior, and inform the competent authority of any work incapacity longer than three months (Article 18(2)).
Inform the competent authority without delay when a driver stops working for them (Article 17).

blocks.text: Drivers have a right to access the data held about them in both registers and to a copy on request (Article 22(3)). A register built from [audit ready training records](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit) makes those requests, and the certified copies required on departure, straightforward.

sections.heading: How can an operator map Directive 2007/59/EC to evidence?

blocks.text: This original mapping links each recurring obligation to the role, frequency and evidence a national safety authority audit would look for. It focuses on what the employer controls, since the license itself is managed by the competent authority. The examinations work much like a formal [verification of competency](/guides/how-to-set-up-verification-of-competency) cycle.

blocks.text: Yes. As at November 2026 the directive is in force, and the most recent amending act listed on EUR-Lex is Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/554, which replaced point 8 of Annex VI to allow pilot projects using alternative language competences. Earlier amendments were made by Commission Directive 2014/82/EU and Commission Directive (EU) 2016/882.

Under the pilot project rules, the Commission may grant a derogation from the B1 language requirement for a limited period not exceeding 36 months in total, and participants must keep records, including the training staff received, for 24 months after the project ends. Directive 2007/59/EC also lets Member States exclude drivers operating only on metros, trams and light rail, functionally separate local networks, private freight infrastructure, or track temporarily closed for maintenance (Article 2(3)). Light rail operators should therefore check national law rather than assume the directive applies.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models the Annex IV, V and VI subjects as separate knowledge areas tied to each certificate entry, so a three yearly route or rolling stock check can be planned against exactly what a driver is authorized for. Because the structure belongs to the driver record, the certified copies owed on departure come from the same source as the audit evidence.

faqs.q: Is a train driver license valid in every EU Member State?
faqs.a: Yes. Article 7 of Directive 2007/59/EC makes the license valid throughout the EU, except a license issued to a driver aged 18 or 19, which is valid only in the issuing Member State. The certificate is different: it is valid only for the infrastructure and rolling stock named on it.

faqs.q: Who sets how often route knowledge is rechecked?
faqs.a: The railway undertaking or infrastructure manager sets the frequency in its safety management system under Article 16(2), but it cannot be less frequent than the Annex VII minimum of every three years, or after an absence of more than one year from the relevant route.

faqs.q: Does Directive 2007/59/EC require drug and alcohol testing?
faqs.a: It does not set a testing program. Annex II lists drug tests where clinically indicated in periodic medicals, and Article 18(2) requires employers to ensure that drivers are never under the influence of any substance likely to affect concentration, attention or behavior. Testing regimes come from national law and the employer's safety management system.

faqs.q: Can training for the certificate be delivered by the employer?
faqs.a: Yes, if the employer or its training provider is accredited or recognized under Article 20. Training on infrastructure knowledge must be delivered by persons or bodies accredited or recognized by the Member State where the infrastructure is located, and safety management system training is the employer's responsibility under Article 13(3).

Minimum license age 20, or 18 with validity limited to the issuing Member State (Article 10); nine years education and level 3 basic training (Article 11)
License issued within one month of complete documents and valid for 10 years (Article 14)
Medical examinations at least every three years up to 55 then yearly; resting ECG for drivers over 40; drug tests where clinically indicated (Annex II sections 3.1 and 3.2)
Annex VII minimum frequencies: language every three years or after absence over one year; infrastructure every three years or after absence over one year on the route; rolling stock every three years
Language competence at level B1 of the CEFR; pilot project derogations up to 36 months; pilot records kept 24 months (Annex VI point 8)
